asBirthCard.p: This one comes from the birthdate alone, so it has nothing to do with your Sun, Moon or rising sign. Add every digit of the date, keep adding until the total is 22 or under, and yours landed on twelve, either straight away or by way of 39, 48 or 57. Twelve is a one and a two, and those add to three, The Empress, the card of things growing, which is worth remembering with a card that looks this still. It comes after Justice, who has just weighed something up, and before Death, where something actually ends. So The Hanged Man is the stretch after the verdict and before the change, and in the picture he's upside down by one ankle and doesn't seem especially bothered. The card's planet is Neptune, which rules Pisces, the twelfth sign. It's in detriment in Virgo, which means it does worst in the sign of lists, deadlines and exact amounts. Deadlines trip up a lot of twelves as well.

You're usually the last one to decide. At a work meeting everyone's got a view by the second slide and you're still turning it over, and then two days later you send an email that changes the whole plan, because you came at it from the other end. A group chat about where to go for dinner can sit unanswered on your side for hours, and it isn't that you don't care, you genuinely can't tell yet. People find that maddening and occasionally very useful. On a free Saturday you can lie on the couch half the afternoon without a phone in your hand and call it a good day. You also tend to put things down for a while, a book, a friendship, a half-finished degree, and pick them up years later as if hardly any time had passed.

Most people are terrible at waiting. They refresh the inbox, ring the agent again, invent a story so there's something to do. You're oddly good at it, and that turns out to be useful to other people. A friend is waiting to hear about the job interview, or the visa, or whether the house sale went through, and you're the one they want around, because you don't fill the gap with guesses. You'll make tea and talk about something else and let the not-knowing sit there in the room with you both. The same thing helps in a negotiation or a family argument. You can leave a silence alone long enough that the other person finally says what they meant. Friends tend to ring you in those weeks, sometimes before they've told anyone else.

The less obvious trouble is that waiting can become a way of choosing without having to say so. You don't break up, you just stop suggesting plans until the other person ends it. The promotion goes to someone else because the application deadline slid past. The lease renews itself because you never got round to giving notice. Then if it goes badly, well, it wasn't really your decision, and that's a very comfortable place to stand. Neptune, the card's planet, doesn't help, since fog is what it's best at. Ask you straight out what you want and you'll say you don't mind, and sometimes that's true, and sometimes you just don't want to be the one who wanted it. The people close to you can usually tell which it is before you can.

When something goes wrong you tend to go still first. Bad news on a Tuesday and you might not tell anyone until the weekend, and in between you carry on with the dishes and the emails as though you're fine, while most of you has gone somewhere else. A week on you're usually sleeping a lot or very little, and you've started giving things away, taking on extra at work, covering a friend's shifts, lending money you haven't got, as if being useful to somebody will make the bad thing make sense. The people around you find it hard because there's nothing to grab hold of. You're not angry and you're not crying. You're just a bit absent. What helps is one person you tell early, and something physical with a start and an end, a swim, or a long walk to a particular place and back.

You're often the one who sees someone from an odd angle and spots the version of them nobody else has noticed yet. The shy colleague who turns out to be very funny. The person everyone wrote off after the divorce. That's lovely, and it's how plenty of twelves end up in long, good relationships their friends didn't see coming. The catch is that you can fall for the version you've spotted and then hang on for it to turn up, longer than most people would. You'll also soak up a partner's moods until you can't tell whose bad day it is, and after a hard week you may need an evening alone to sort out which feelings are yours. Every so often, ask yourself whether you're with the person in front of you or the one you're hoping for, and say so out loud if it's the second.

Work with waiting built into it suits you better than you'd expect. Research, editing, anything with long lead times, planning work where a file sits for a month and then needs someone who still remembers it. You're good at the second look, the one nobody budgeted for, and twelves often end up as the person who spots what's wrong with the plan everyone else has signed off. The strain comes in workplaces that reward whoever talks first, because you'll often have the better idea and say it on Thursday. The other trouble is vagueness. You end up covering half of someone's role after they leave, or doing a job that never had a proper description, and because nobody wrote it down, nobody pays you for it. Keep a list of what you've agreed to do, and treat anything outside it as a favour you're choosing to give.

At twenty a twelve often feels behind. Friends have picked a course, a city, a partner, and you're still working out what you think, and people tell you you'll get there in a tone you don't love. There's often a stretch in the twenties where life stalls for a year or two, a family member who needs looking after, a job that holds you in place, and it feels like wasted time. By the mid-thirties most twelves can look back and see the stuck year was where the real decision got made. The fifties tend to bring a better ear for when a wait is doing some good and when it's only habit. Quite a few twelves make their biggest late change around then, a move or a new line of work they'd sat on for ten years, and they make it fast, which surprises everyone.

When you notice you're waiting on something, a reply, a decision, someone else's move, write it on a sticky note with a date beside it, the date by which you'll act whether or not anything has changed. Stick it inside a kitchen cupboard door where you'll see it most mornings. When the date comes, do the thing, even if it's only sending one message. Keep the old notes in a drawer. After a year or so you'll be able to look through them and see which of the waits were worth it.
